📌 Russian Operations Focus on Ukrainian Logistics as Drone War Intensifies

🔶 Long-Range Strikes
Russia continued long-range strikes against targets in the Odesa region, including naval facilities near the ports. Attack drones also struck fuel depots and logistics sites, including the Epicenter hypermarket in Sumy, as part of efforts to disrupt Ukrainian supply networks.
🔶 Ukrainian Drone Campaign
Ukraine maintained a high tempo of drone attacks. Russia claimed to have intercepted 161 Ukrainian UAVs in one day. Drones reportedly struck logistics facilities in the Moscow and Lipetsk regions, while Crimea and Sevastopol were also targeted overnight.

🔶 Belgorod and Bryansk
Civilian casualties were reported in Russia's border regions. In Shebekino, Belgorod region, a bus strike reportedly killed five people and injured 23. Additional attacks across Belgorod left several more civilians dead and wounded. In Bryansk, a firefighter was killed and several civilians were injured in separate strikes.
🔶 Sumy Border
Heavy fighting continued along the Sumy border. Clashes were reported around Ulanovo, Malaya Sloboda, Ryzhevka, Pisarevka, Mogritsa, Maryino, Novaya Sech, Khoten, and Prokhody, with both sides engaged in ongoing firefights.

🔶 Kursk
A Ukrainian drone strike near the railway station in Lgov reportedly injured five railway workers. Rail operations at the station were temporarily suspended under the counter-terrorism regime.
🔶 Kupyansk
Fighting continued around Kupyansk as Ukrainian forces reportedly attempted to reinforce the area. No major territorial changes were reported farther south.

🔶 Konstantinovka–Dobropolye
Russian sources claimed clearing operations continued in Konstantinovka. In the Dobropolye direction, fighting was reported around Belitskoye while Russian forces expanded their control around the previously captured village of Mirne.
🔶 Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia
Russian sources claimed the capture of Volnoye in Dnipropetrovsk region. West of Rovne and Kopani in Zaporizhzhia, Russian units reportedly broke through Ukrainian defensive positions and consolidated newly gained ground.

🔶 Kherson
Russian-controlled areas of Kherson remained under Ukrainian drone attacks. Authorities reported civilian casualties in Skadovsk and damage to infrastructure across several settlements, including Antonovka, Nova Kakhovka, Kalanchak, and Hola Prystan.
Forward assessment: Drone strikes and long-range attacks are likely to continue as both sides focus on disrupting logistics while ground fighting remains active.

Personal analysis: The battlefield remains dominated by attrition. Both Russia and Ukraine continue targeting logistics, infrastructure, and rear areas while seeking limited tactical gains along multiple sectors.

post.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky shared a cordial but serious conversation and handshake Tuesday before the funeral of Sen. Lindsey Graham, marking their first in-person meeting since September 2023. Both leaders had met separately with President Trump at the White House earlier in the day. 

Graham was one of Congress’ strongest advocates for both Israel and Ukraine, consistently pressing for robust U.S. military and financial support for the two allies throughout their wars.

While relations between Jerusalem and Kyiv have often been complicated by Israel’s effort to avoid directly confronting Russia, the two countries are increasingly united by a common challenge: Iran. Over the weekend, Ukraine targeted at least one Iranian-linked vessel in the Caspian Sea that Kyiv says was supporting Russia’s war effort. 

The evolving battlefield has also created new opportunities for cooperation. Ukraine has long sought Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system, while Israel could benefit from Kyiv’s experience countering the cheap Iranian-designed Shahed drones that Russia has deployed throughout the war. Ukraine has increasingly relied on low-cost interceptor drones and electronic warfare—capabilities that could help Israel reduce its reliance on expensive missile interceptors against relatively inexpensive Iranian drones. So far, however, the two countries have not announced any major defense agreements.

post.text:
🇺🇲 The U.S. Marine Corps is racing to build what Ukraine has already proven on the battlefield: an army where small FPV attack drones become standard weapons carried by frontline troops.
According to the Wall Street Journal, the Marines want 10,000 FPV-capable drones in just the next 12 months, with the ability to carry grenades or mortar rounds.

Instead of waiting for artillery or air support, platoons and squads will be able to identify a target, launch a precision strike within minutes, and immediately continue the assault.

The goal is changing how infantry fights. Ukraine fundamentally changed military thinking.

The Marines are now training with Neros Archer FPV drones in Australia as part of preparations for a potential Indo-Pacific conflict. The drones cost roughly $2,000–5,000 each, can be operated directly by frontline Marines through FPV goggles, and are expected to complement anti-ship missiles, surveillance assets and distributed island operations.

Production is accelerating rapidly. Neros says it currently builds around 1,400 drones per week and aims to reach 1 million annually by 2028.

Challenges remain - from logistics and weather to scaling production - but one lesson from Ukraine is now impossible to ignore: the era when only expensive missiles and aircraft delivered precision strikes is ending. Cheap, expendable FPV drones are becoming a core battlefield capability.

🎯🔥 GUNNY’S THREE-ROUND REPORT
ROUND THREE • EVENING DEBRIEF
KYIV TAKES MISSILE FIRE AS THE LOGISTICS WAR SPREADS

Mission Snapshot: Tonight’s real developments are not the recycled clips and engagement bait flying around social media. Kyiv came under a renewed ballistic-missile attack, Ukraine’s long-range campaign is hitting Russian logistics infrastructure, and a major chemical-facility fire in Brazil created a serious public-safety emergency.

1️⃣ KYIV UNDER RENEWED BALLISTIC-MISSILE ATTACK

✅ Confirmed: Russia launched waves of ballistic-missile attacks against Kyiv early August 5 local time, according to Reuters and Kyiv officials.

🔥 Fires were reported at residential buildings, warehouses, and locations on the city’s outskirts. Air defenses were active as the attack unfolded.

⚠️ Initial reports did not confirm casualties. That can change fast after emergency crews reach damaged sites.

Why it matters: This is not a symbolic strike. Ballistic missiles compress warning time, put civilian areas at direct risk, and keep pressure on Ukraine’s capital while the war’s political and diplomatic tracks remain unsettled.

Watch next: casualty figures, damage assessments, and whether Russia follows this attack with a wider drone or missile wave.

2️⃣ UKRAINE IS TAKING THE LOGISTICS FIGHT INSIDE RUSSIA

✅ Confirmed: Ukraine has struck Russian warehouse and logistics targets, including a confirmed fire at a Wildberries logistics facility in Krasny Bor, Leningrad Oblast, near St. Petersburg.

🔄 Correction: Do not share the social-media claim that tonight’s footage showed an attack on an Aleksin, Tula Wildberries center. The confirmed warehouse fire was near St. Petersburg—not Aleksin.

🎯 What matters: Both sides are targeting the machinery that keeps war moving: warehouses, transport routes, fuel, production, and distribution hubs. A warehouse is not just boxes on shelves when it can support military supply chains, national commerce, or wartime logistics.

🗣️ Ukrainian adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov has argued Russia is increasingly targeting commercial and logistical infrastructure in Ukraine. That is his assessment—not independent proof of every claimed target.

3️⃣ CHEMICAL-FACILITY FIRE ROCKS GREATER SÃO PAULO

✅ **Confirmed:** A major fire broke out at Quema Química, a solvent and resin facility in Itaquaquecetuba, Greater São Paulo.

💥 The fire reached solvent storage and triggered multiple secondary explosions. Authorities reported explosions in storm-drain/manhole infrastructure after chemicals entered the drainage system.

🚒 At least 60 firefighters and roughly 30 emergency vehicles responded. Nearby buildings were evacuated, and officials warned of potentially toxic smoke and a possible chemical leak.

✅ No injuries were reported in the latest update.

❓ The cause remains unknown. There is no evidence at this point of sabotage or an attack.
Bottom line: Call this what it is—a chemical-plant fire with multiple explosions. Do not twist it into “the plant exploded” or pretend there is evidence of an attack.

⚡ RAPID-FIRE UPDATES

🇮🇱🇮🇷 Hormuz pressure: Israel is reportedly receiving indirect updates—not direct participation—on negotiations involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. An unnamed Israeli official told N12 that Israel fears Washington may push too hard for a deal. That is an Israeli assessment, not confirmation of U.S. policy or a completed agreement.

🇰🇷 Osan Air Base: Eight South Korean students were reportedly detained after allegedly entering Osan Air Base and shouting anti-U.S. slogans. Police are investigating under laws protecting military installations. The allegation remains subject to the investigation.

🌕 SpaceX upper stage: A spent Falcon 9 upper stage is expected to impact the Moon near Einstein Crater overnight. No danger to Earth—and likely not much to see from here.

❓ Dubai smoke/“three explosions”: Still unverified. Videos show smoke near the Jebel Ali industrial area, but there is no confirmed cause, strike, casualty count, or connection to Iran/Hormuz. Hold the line until UAE authorities or reliable reporting confirms it.

🔄 Recycle bin: The Rozetka warehouse footage circulating as “breaking” is old. The facility was struck August 1–2. It does not belong in tonight’s breaking-news feed.

📋 CONFIRMATION BOARD

✅ Newly confirmed: Kyiv ballistic-missile attack; Wildberries logistics fire near St. Petersburg; chemical-facility emergency near São Paulo.

🔄 Corrected: Wildberries fire was not confirmed in Aleksin, Tula. Rozetka footage is not fresh.

⚠️ Still developing: Kyiv damage and casualty assessments; Brazil fire containment and environmental risk.

❓ Unverified: Dubai explosion claims and any claimed link to the regional Iran/Hormuz crisis.

🎯 GUNNY’S TAKE

The battlefield is no longer just trenches, tanks, and front lines. It is warehouses, freight, drones, fuel, apartment blocks, industrial sites, and the systems that let a country keep functioning under war.

But that is exactly why accuracy matters. A real strike does not need a fake location. A real fire does not need an invented sabotage story. And smoke in a video is not automatically a missile, an explosion, or the start of World War III.

The pressure is real. The rumor mill is real too. Learn the damn difference.
What deserves more attention right now: Russia’s attacks on Kyiv, or the expanding war on logistics inside Russia?

🚨 DRONE STRIKES CLAIM MASSIVE RUSSIAN LOSSES IN JULY.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukrainian drones eliminated 30,272 Russian soldiers in July. He says every case is backed by clear video proof. The figure includes both killed and badly wounded troops.

Zelensky shared the numbers after reviewing reports from the Defense Ministry and the Security Service of Ukraine. He said the trend on the front has stayed the same for months, with Russia losing about 30,000 troops monthly. He also praised the SBU’s Alpha unit for leading July’s drone strikes.

Ukraine has leaned heavily on drones as the war enters its third year. The country’s unmanned units have hit tens of thousands of targets each month. July’s tally matches earlier reports from May and June, showing a steady pace of drone‑inflicted losses.

Zelensky urged partners to keep supplying air‑defense missiles. He said each delivery saves lives as Russia continues heavy missile attacks. He warned that the coming winter could bring more strikes on Ukraine’s energy and water systems.

The claim highlights how drones have reshaped modern warfare. Ukraine’s drone fleet has grown fast, and its battlefield impact now rivals traditional artillery in some sectors. The July numbers, if accurate, mark one of the largest monthly personnel losses ever recorded in the conflict.

As part of this cooperation, Ukraine’s defense industry is reportedly set to reverse-engineer 5V55R and 9M83 surface-to-air missiles used by the S-300P and S-300V1 families.

The 5V55R is used by the S-300P family, including the S-300PT and S-300PS, while the 9M83 is an interceptor of the S-300V1 system.

With European assistance, the missiles are expected to receive new onboard radar seekers/receivers while remaining compatible with their respective launchers.

Remaining stocks of 5V55R and 9M83 missiles are also planned for refurbishment and return to service. Some have become unusable due to the age and degradation of their batteries.

Ukraine has previously upgraded the 5V55R, extending its range from 75 km to 150 km.

Overall, the effort could help partially alleviate Ukraine’s shortage of Patriot air-defense systems.
